1.4: A balanced chemical equation has an equal number of atoms of each element on both the reactant and product sides (e.g., 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O). Chemical equations must be balanced to satisfy the Law of Conservation of Mass — mass (atoms) can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction.

(b) 2NaOH + H₂SO₄ → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O
(c) NaCl + AgNO₃ → AgCl + NaNO₃ (already balanced)
(d) BaCl₂ + H₂SO₄ → BaSO₄ + 2HCl

(a) Ca(OH)₂(aq) + CO₂(g) → CaCO₃(s) + H₂O(l)
(b) Zn(s) + 2AgNO₃(aq) → Zn(NO₃)₂(aq) + 2Ag(s)

(b) ZnCO₃(s) → ZnO(s) + CO₂(g) — Thermal decomposition reaction.
(c) H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2HCl(g) — Combination reaction.
(d) Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g) — Displacement reaction.
1.9: Exothermic reactions release heat along with the formation of products — e.g., burning of natural gas: CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(g) + Heat; respiration. Endothermic reactions absorb energy (heat, light or electricity) from the surroundings — e.g., CaCO₃(s) + Heat → CaO(s) + CO₂(g); N₂(g) + O₂(g) + Heat → 2NO(g).
1.10: During digestion, carbohydrates are broken down into glucose. In cells, glucose combines with oxygen to form carbon dioxide and water while releasing energy (ATP + heat): C₆H₁₂O₆(aq) + 6O₂(aq) → 6CO₂(aq) + 6H₂O(l) + Energy. Since energy is released, respiration is an exothermic reaction.
1.11: In a combination reaction, two or more substances combine to form a single product (e.g., 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l)), whereas in a decomposition reaction, a single compound breaks down into two or more simpler substances using energy (e.g., 2H₂O(l) --(electricity)--> 2H₂(g) + O₂(g)). Hence they are opposites.
1.12:
• By heat (thermolysis): CaCO₃(s) --(Heat)--> CaO(s) + CO₂(g)
• By light (photolysis): 2AgCl(s) --(Sunlight)--> 2Ag(s) + Cl₂(g)
• By electricity (electrolysis): 2H₂O(l) --(Electric current)--> 2H₂(g) + O₂(g)
1.13: In a displacement reaction, a more reactive element displaces a less reactive element from its salt solution: Zn(s) + CuSO₄(aq) → ZnSO₄(aq) + Cu(s). In a double displacement reaction, two compounds exchange ions in solution to form new compounds (often a precipitate): Na₂SO₄(aq) + BaCl₂(aq) → BaSO₄(s)↓ + 2NaCl(aq).
1.14: Cu(s) + 2AgNO₃(aq) → Cu(NO₃)₂(aq) + 2Ag(s). Copper, being more reactive than silver, displaces silver metal from silver nitrate solution.
1.15: Any reaction that produces an insoluble solid (precipitate) which separates out from the solution is called a precipitation reaction. Examples: (1) Na₂SO₄(aq) + BaCl₂(aq) → BaSO₄(s)↓ (white ppt.) + 2NaCl(aq); (2) AgNO₃(aq) + NaCl(aq) → AgCl(s)↓ (white ppt.) + NaNO₃(aq).
1.16:
(a) Oxidation is the gain of oxygen by a substance. Examples: (1) 2Cu + O₂ --(Heat)--> 2CuO (copper oxidised to CuO); (2) C + O₂ → CO₂ (carbon oxidised to CO₂).
(b) Reduction is the loss of oxygen from a substance. Examples: (1) CuO + H₂ --(Heat)--> Cu + H₂O (CuO reduced to Cu); (2) ZnO + C → Zn + CO (ZnO reduced to Zn).
1.17: Element ‘X’ is Copper (Cu). On heating in air it forms black Copper(II) oxide (CuO): 2Cu(s) + O₂(g) --(Heat)--> 2CuO(s).
1.18: Paint forms a protective coating on the surface of iron and cuts off direct contact with air (oxygen) and moisture, thereby preventing rusting (corrosion) of iron.
1.19: Oils and fats get oxidised in contact with oxygen and become rancid (foul smell and taste). Flushing packets with unreactive nitrogen gas displaces oxygen and acts as an antioxidant, preventing rancidity.
1.20:
(a) Corrosion: Slow deterioration of metals when attacked by air, moisture or acids around them. Example: Rusting of iron (formation of reddish-brown hydrated ferric oxide, Fe₂O₃·xH₂O), or black coating of Ag₂S on silver.
(b) Rancidity: Oxidation of fats and oils in food when left exposed to air, causing unpleasant smell and taste. Example: Potato chips or butter turning stale and foul-smelling when kept open.

2.7: Distilled water is pure and contains no dissolved ionic salts or free ions to carry charge. Rainwater dissolves atmospheric gases like CO₂ (forming carbonic acid, H₂CO₃) and traces of SO₂/NO₂, producing free H⁺ and anion charge carriers that conduct electricity.
2.8: Acidic behaviour is due to hydrogen/hydronium ions (H⁺(aq) or H₃O⁺). Separation of H⁺ ions from acid molecules (like HCl) cannot occur without water molecules (HCl + H₂O → H₃O⁺ + Cl⁻); hence dry acids do not show acidic properties.

2.13: Plaster of Paris (CaSO₄·½H₂O) readily absorbs moisture from air and hydrates into hard solid gypsum, losing its setting property: CaSO₄·½H₂O + 1½H₂O → CaSO₄·2H₂O (Gypsum). Therefore it must be stored in a moisture-proof container.
2.14: The reaction between an acid and a base to form salt and water is called a neutralisation reaction (H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l)). Examples: (1) NaOH(aq) + HCl(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l); (2) KOH(aq) + HNO₃(aq) → KNO₃(aq) + H₂O(l).
2.15:
Uses of washing soda (Na₂CO₃·10H₂O): (1) Used in glass, soap and paper industries; (2) Used for removing permanent hardness of water (and as a domestic cleaning agent).
Uses of baking soda (NaHCO₃): (1) Used in making baking powder (for spongy cakes/bread) and as an antacid to relieve acidity; (2) Used in soda-acid fire extinguishers.

(ii) Electrical circuit test: Connect each sample between battery, bulb and switch — the bulb glows with metals (good conductors) and generally does not glow with non-metals.

3.6: Metal oxides which react with both acids and bases to produce salt and water are called amphoteric oxides. Examples: Aluminium oxide (Al₂O₃) and Zinc oxide (ZnO). For Al₂O₃: Al₂O₃ + 6HCl → 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂O; Al₂O₃ + 2NaOH → 2NaAlO₂ + H₂O.
3.7:
Metals that displace hydrogen from dilute acids (above H in reactivity series): Zinc (Zn) and Magnesium (Mg) [also Fe, Al].
Metals that do NOT displace hydrogen from dilute acids (below H): Copper (Cu) and Silver (Ag) [also Au, Hg].
3.8:

3.10: Two ways to prevent rusting of iron: (1) Galvanisation — coating iron articles with a thin layer of zinc; (2) Painting, oiling, greasing, chrome plating or alloying (making stainless steel) to prevent contact with air and moisture.
3.11: Non-metals combine with oxygen to form acidic oxides (e.g., CO₂, SO₂, NO₂) or neutral oxides (e.g., CO, H₂O, N₂O).
3.12:
(a) Platinum, gold and silver are very lustrous, highly malleable and ductile, and least reactive — they do not corrode or tarnish easily.
(b) Sodium, potassium and lithium are extremely reactive; they react vigorously with oxygen and moisture in air and catch fire, so they are stored under kerosene/paraffin oil.
(c) Aluminium forms a tough, thin, non-porous protective layer of aluminium oxide (Al₂O₃) that prevents further corrosion, and it is a good conductor of heat.
(d) It is much easier to obtain a metal by reducing its oxide than directly from its carbonate or sulphide; hence carbonates (by calcination) and sulphides (by roasting) are first converted to oxides.
3.13: Copper reacts slowly with moist CO₂ in air to form a dull green coating of basic copper carbonate (CuCO₃·Cu(OH)₂). Lemon and tamarind juice contain acids (citric/tartaric acid) which neutralise and dissolve this basic layer, restoring copper’s shine, while not reacting with copper metal itself.
3.14:
1. Metals form basic or amphoteric oxides (e.g., Na₂O, Al₂O₃); non-metals form acidic or neutral oxides (e.g., CO₂, CO).
2. Reactive metals displace H₂ from dilute acids and water; non-metals do not displace H₂ from dilute acids.
3. Metals are electropositive (lose electrons to form cations, acting as reducing agents); non-metals are electronegative (gain/share electrons, acting as oxidising agents).
3.15: He used Aqua Regia — a freshly prepared 3:1 mixture of concentrated hydrochloric acid (HCl) and concentrated nitric acid (HNO₃). Though neither acid alone dissolves gold, aqua regia is highly corrosive and dissolves the outer layer of gold, exposing a shiny inner surface while reducing the bangles’ weight.
3.16: Copper does not react with cold water, hot water or steam, and is an excellent conductor of heat. Steel contains iron, which reacts with steam formed from hot water (3Fe + 4H₂O(g) → Fe₃O₄ + 4H₂) and corrodes over time. Hence copper is preferred.

4.4: Carbon (atomic no. 6; 2,4) needs 4 electrons to complete its octet; each H (1) needs 1 electron for its duplet; Cl (2,8,7) needs 1 electron for its octet. Carbon shares three valence electrons with three H atoms (three C–H single covalent bonds) and its fourth valence electron with one Cl atom (one C–Cl single covalent bond), forming covalent CH₃Cl in which every atom attains a noble-gas configuration.
4.5:
(a) Ethanoic acid (CH₃COOH): Methyl carbon forms 3 single bonds with H and 1 single bond with carboxyl carbon; carboxyl carbon forms a double bond (=O, 2 shared pairs) with one O (having 2 lone pairs) and a single bond with –OH oxygen (having 2 lone pairs and 1 single bond to H).
(b) H₂S: Sulphur (6 valence e⁻) shares 1 electron pair with each of two H atoms (H–S–H) and retains 2 lone pairs.
(c) Propanone (CH₃COCH₃): Central carbonyl carbon forms single bonds to two –CH₃ groups and a double bond (2 shared pairs) to oxygen (2 lone pairs).
(d) F₂: Each F atom (7 valence e⁻) shares 1 electron pair to form F–F, with 3 lone pairs on each F atom.
4.6: A homologous series is a family of organic compounds having the same functional group and similar chemical properties in which successive members differ by a –CH₂– unit (14 u molecular mass) and show a regular gradation in physical properties. Example: Alkanes (CₙH₂ₙ₊₂) — CH₄, C₂H₆, C₃H₈, C₄H₁₀; or Alcohols — CH₃OH, C₂H₅OH, C₃H₇OH.
4.7:
Physical properties: (1) Ethanol has a pleasant smell and burning taste, whereas ethanoic acid has a pungent vinegar-like smell and sour taste; (2) Melting point of ethanol is 156 K vs 290 K for ethanoic acid (which freezes in winter as glacial acetic acid).
Chemical properties: (1) Ethanoic acid turns blue litmus red; ethanol is neutral to litmus. (2) Ethanoic acid reacts with NaHCO₃/Na₂CO₃ giving brisk effervescence of CO₂ gas (CH₃COOH + NaHCO₃ → CH₃COONa + H₂O + CO₂↑), whereas ethanol does not react.
4.8: A soap molecule has two ends: a hydrophilic (water-loving) ionic head (–COO⁻Na⁺) and a hydrophobic (water-repelling) long hydrocarbon tail. In water, hydrophobic tails cluster inward away from water while ionic heads point outward into water, forming spherical micelles. Micelles will NOT form in ethanol because the hydrocarbon tail is soluble in ethanol.
4.9: Carbon and its compounds undergo combustion in oxygen to form CO₂ and H₂O while releasing a large amount of heat and light energy (high calorific value), have moderate ignition temperatures, burn cleanly when supplied sufficient oxygen, and their combustion is easy to control.
4.10: Hard water contains dissolved calcium (Ca²⁺) and magnesium (Mg²⁺) salts. Soap (sodium/potassium salt of long-chain fatty acids, e.g., C₁₇H₃₅COONa) reacts with Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ ions to form insoluble curdy white precipitates of calcium and magnesium salts of fatty acids called scum: 2C₁₇H₃₅COONa + Ca²⁺ → (C₁₇H₃₅COO)₂Ca↓ (scum) + 2Na⁺.
4.11: Soap solution is basic (alkaline) in nature (salt of a weak fatty acid and strong base NaOH/KOH). Hence it turns red litmus paper blue and leaves blue litmus paper unchanged.
4.12: Hydrogenation is the addition of hydrogen (H₂) to unsaturated hydrocarbons in the presence of catalysts such as nickel (Ni) or palladium (Pd) to form saturated hydrocarbons. Industrial application: Conversion of liquid unsaturated vegetable oils into solid saturated fats (vanaspati ghee) using a nickel catalyst.
4.13: C₃H₆ (propene, an alkene CₙH₂ₙ) and C₂H₂ (ethyne, an alkyne CₙH₂ₙ₋₂) undergo addition reactions because they are unsaturated hydrocarbons containing double/triple carbon-carbon bonds. C₂H₆, C₃H₈ and CH₄ are saturated alkanes.
4.14:
(1) Bromine water test: Unsaturated hydrocarbons decolourise reddish-brown bromine water by addition, whereas saturated hydrocarbons do not.
(2) Flame test: Saturated hydrocarbons generally burn with a clean blue flame, while unsaturated hydrocarbons burn with a yellow sooty flame.
4.15: Most dirt is oily in nature and insoluble in water. When soap dissolves in water, its hydrophobic hydrocarbon tails attach to the oily dirt droplet while its hydrophilic ionic heads (–COO⁻Na⁺) face outward into water, forming a micelle trapping the oil at the centre. Mutual ion-ion repulsion keeps micelles dispersed as an emulsion; on agitation and rinsing with water, the trapped oily dirt is washed away.

5.5: Fats are digested in the small intestine. Bile juice from the liver makes the medium alkaline and emulsifies large fat globules into tiny droplets (increasing surface area). Then the enzyme lipase (from pancreatic and intestinal juice) breaks down emulsified fats into fatty acids and glycerol.
5.6: Saliva moistens and softens food for easy chewing and swallowing, and contains the enzyme salivary amylase (ptyalin) which breaks down complex starch molecules into simpler sugar (maltose).
5.7: Necessary conditions for autotrophic nutrition (photosynthesis): carbon dioxide (CO₂), water (H₂O), sunlight and chlorophyll. Its by-products are oxygen (O₂) and water (along with glucose synthesised as food): 6CO₂ + 12H₂O --(Sunlight, Chlorophyll)--> C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ + 6H₂O.
5.8: Aerobic respiration occurs in presence of O₂ (cytoplasm + mitochondria), completely oxidises glucose to CO₂ and H₂O, and yields large energy (38/36 ATP). Anaerobic respiration occurs in absence of O₂ (cytoplasm only), incompletely breaks glucose into ethanol + CO₂ (in yeast) or lactic acid (in muscles), and yields very little energy (2 ATP). Anaerobic organisms: Yeast and certain anaerobic bacteria.
5.9: Lungs contain millions of tiny balloon-like alveoli providing an enormous surface area (~80 m²); their walls are one-cell thick (squamous epithelium) for rapid diffusion, moist, and richly supplied with an extensive network of blood capillaries.
5.10: Haemoglobin is the respiratory pigment in RBCs that transports oxygen from the lungs to all body tissues. Its deficiency (anaemia) reduces the oxygen-carrying capacity of blood, leading to lower cellular energy production, fatigue, breathlessness, weakness and pale skin.
5.11: In human double circulation, blood passes through the heart twice in one complete cycle: (1) Pulmonary circulation (heart → lungs → heart for oxygenation) and (2) Systemic circulation (heart → body organs → heart to supply O₂). It is necessary to prevent mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood, ensuring highly efficient O₂ supply to meet the high energy needs of warm-blooded humans (maintaining constant body temperature).
5.12:
1. Xylem transports water and dissolved minerals; phloem transports prepared food (sucrose), amino acids and hormones.
2. Xylem flow is unidirectional (roots upward to shoots); phloem translocation is bidirectional (upward and downward).
3. Xylem relies mainly on physical forces (root pressure and transpiration pull) without ATP; phloem uses active transport requiring energy (ATP).
5.13: Alveoli (functional units of lungs) are thin-walled balloon-like air sacs surrounded by capillaries; they exchange O₂ and CO₂ between inhaled air and blood by diffusion. Nephrons (functional units of kidneys) are tubular units with Bowman’s capsule (containing glomerulus capillaries) and coiled renal tubule; they filter nitrogenous wastes (urea, uric acid) from blood and selectively reabsorb glucose, amino acids, salts and water to form urine. Both possess huge numbers, vast surface area and dense capillary networks.

6.4: Receptors are specialised cells in sense organs that detect environmental stimuli (e.g., gustatory for taste, olfactory for smell, photoreceptors for light, thermoreceptors for heat) and generate nerve impulses. If receptors fail (e.g., blocked nose during a cold, damaged skin thermoreceptors), the body cannot sense spoiled food, gas leaks or hot objects, risking injury or harm.
6.5: A neuron consists of: (1) Dendrites — branched projections receiving information; (2) Cell body (cyton) — containing nucleus and cytoplasm; (3) Axon — long fibre conducting electrical nerve impulses away from the cell body; and (4) Nerve endings — releasing neurotransmitters across the synapse to the next neuron, muscle or gland, enabling rapid signal transmission.
6.6: Phototropism is directional growth in response to light. When light falls on one side of a plant shoot, the hormone auxin (synthesised at the shoot tip) diffuses towards the shaded side. Higher auxin concentration stimulates cells on the shaded side to elongate more than those on the lit side, causing the shoot to bend towards light.
6.7: In a spinal cord injury: (1) Reflex actions mediated by the spinal cord are disrupted; and (2) Both sensory impulses travelling from body receptors to the brain and motor impulses travelling from the brain to muscles/effectors below the injury site are disrupted.
6.8: Plants lack a nervous system and coordinate using chemical messengers called plant hormones (phytohormones), synthesised in one region and diffusing to target sites: Auxins (cell elongation, tropism), Gibberellins (stem growth), Cytokinins (cell division), and Abscisic acid (growth inhibitor, wilting of leaves, stomatal closure).
6.9: Multicellular organisms have specialised organs and tissues that must work together in an integrated manner, and must respond accurately and promptly to environmental changes (stimuli) for protection, homeostasis, growth and survival — requiring nervous and hormonal control and coordination.
6.10: Involuntary actions are automatic ongoing internal processes (like heartbeat, breathing, peristalsis, blood pressure) controlled mainly by the mid-brain and hind-brain (medulla) without an external emergency stimulus. Reflex actions are sudden, rapid, automatic responses to a specific external stimulus (like pulling hand away from a hot object) mediated directly by the spinal cord via a reflex arc.
6.11: Nervous mechanism sends electrical impulses along neurons (with neurotransmitters at synapses): very fast, highly localised (reaches only innervated cells), and short-lived. Hormonal (endocrine) mechanism secretes hormones into blood: slower, widespread (reaches all target cells throughout the body), and longer-lasting/persistent. Both work together via feedback mechanisms.
6.12: Movement in a sensitive plant (Mimosa pudica) is a nastic response with no nerves or muscles: plant cells change shape by rapidly altering their water content (turgor pressure), causing leaves to fold. Movement in our legs is voluntary, controlled by brain and motor neurons, and occurs when muscle cells shorten/change shape using specialised contractile proteins (actin and myosin).

7.4: Sexual reproduction combines DNA from two different individuals, generating greater genetic variation in offspring. These variations increase adaptability to changing environments, improve disease resistance, and ensure long-term survival and evolution of the species, unlike asexual reproduction which produces near-identical clones.
7.5: The testes perform two main functions in human males: (1) Production of male germ-cells (sperms) for reproduction; and (2) Secretion of the male sex hormone testosterone, which regulates sperm formation and brings about secondary sexual characteristics at puberty.
7.6: Every month the ovary releases one egg and the uterus prepares a thick, spongy, blood-rich lining (endometrium) to nourish a potential embryo. If the egg is not fertilised, this lining is no longer needed and breaks down slowly, exiting through the vagina as blood and mucous — called menstruation.
7.7: A longitudinal section (L.S.) of a bisexual flower shows four whorls on the receptacle: (1) Sepals (calyx, green protective outer whorl); (2) Petals (corolla, coloured to attract pollinators); (3) Stamens (male part — anther bearing pollen grains + filament); and (4) Pistil/Carpel (female part — sticky stigma at top, tubular style, and swollen basal ovary containing ovules with female germ-cells).
7.8:
1. Mechanical barrier methods: Condoms or cervical caps prevent sperm from reaching the egg (condoms also protect against STDs).
2. Chemical/hormonal methods: Oral contraceptive pills alter hormonal balance to prevent ovulation.
3. Intrauterine Contraceptive Devices (IUCDs): Copper-T or loop placed in the uterus prevents pregnancy.
4. Surgical (permanent) methods: Vasectomy (blocking vas deferens in males) and Tubectomy (blocking fallopian tubes in females).
7.9: Unicellular organisms consist of a single cell and reproduce mainly by simple asexual methods such as binary fission (Amoeba), multiple fission (Plasmodium) or budding (Yeast). Multicellular organisms have differentiated tissues and specialised reproductive organs, so cell-by-cell division cannot work; they reproduce via complex methods such as spore formation, vegetative propagation or sexual reproduction involving gametes.
7.10: Reproduction creates new individuals carrying the species’ DNA body design to replace organisms lost to ageing, predation and death, maintaining population numbers. Additionally, DNA variations generated during reproduction allow some individuals to survive drastic environmental changes, preventing extinction.
7.11:
1. Preventing unwanted or frequent pregnancies and spacing births.
2. Protecting maternal and child health.
3. Controlling population size and improving family standard of living.
4. Preventing transmission of sexually transmitted diseases (STDs) such as HIV-AIDS, syphilis and gonorrhoea (via barrier methods like condoms).

8.1: Mendel crossed pure tall (TT) pea plants with pure dwarf (tt) plants. All F₁ progeny (Tt) were tall — no dwarf or medium plants appeared, showing tallness (T) is dominant. On self-pollinating F₁ plants, F₂ progeny produced tall and dwarf plants in a 3:1 phenotypic ratio (1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt), proving the dwarf trait (t) was recessive (present in F₁ but expressed only when homozygous tt).
8.2: In a dihybrid cross between pea plants with round-yellow seeds (RRYY) and wrinkled-green seeds (rryy), all F₁ seeds were round-yellow (RrYy). On selfing F₁, the F₂ generation showed a 9:3:3:1 ratio — round-yellow (9), round-green (3), wrinkled-yellow (3), wrinkled-green (1). The appearance of two new non-parental combinations (round-green and wrinkled-yellow) proves seed shape and seed colour assort independently.
8.3: No, this information alone is not sufficient. Case 1: If A is dominant, a heterozygous father (Iᴬi) and mother (ii) can produce a daughter with blood group O (ii). Case 2: If O were dominant, a father (aa) and heterozygous mother (Oo) could also produce a daughter with group O (Oo). Since both hypotheses explain the child’s blood group, dominance cannot be deduced from this single cross alone.
8.4: Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes: 22 autosome pairs and 1 pair of sex chromosomes — XX in females and XY in males. All eggs carry an X chromosome, while half the sperms carry X and half carry Y. If an X-bearing sperm fertilises the egg, the zygote is XX (girl); if a Y-bearing sperm fertilises the egg, the zygote is XY (boy). Thus sex is determined by the chromosome inherited from the father (50:50 chance).

10.8: To focus on closer objects, the ciliary muscles contract to make the eye lens thicker and decrease its focal length. However, the focal length of the eye lens cannot be decreased below a certain minimum limit, so objects placed closer than the near point (~25 cm) cannot be focused sharply on the retina and appear blurred.
10.9: The image distance in the eye remains unchanged (equal to the fixed distance between the eye lens and the retina). As object distance increases, the ciliary muscles relax to increase the focal length of the eye lens (accommodation) so the image continues to form sharply on the retina.
10.10: Stars are very distant point-sized sources of light. Starlight undergoes continuous atmospheric refraction through layers of air of gradually increasing refractive index. Because the atmosphere’s physical conditions (temperature, density) constantly fluctuate, the apparent position of the star and the amount of starlight entering the eye flicker continuously, making stars twinkle.
10.11: Planets are much closer to Earth and appear as extended sources — a collection of a large number of point-sized sources of light. Random variations in light entering the eye from individual point sources cancel out and average to zero, so their apparent brightness stays steady and planets do not twinkle.
10.12: On Earth, the sky looks blue due to scattering of shorter-wavelength blue sunlight by air molecules and fine particles in the atmosphere. In outer space (at an astronaut’s altitude), there is no atmosphere to scatter sunlight into the astronaut’s eyes, so the sky appears dark/black.

11.7: Plotting V (y-axis) against I (x-axis) gives a straight line passing through the origin (verifying Ohm’s law). Resistance R = slope = ΔV/ΔI. Using individual ratios: 1.6/0.5 = 3.2 Ω, 3.4/1.0 = 3.4 Ω, 6.7/2.0 = 3.35 Ω, 10.2/3.0 = 3.4 Ω, 13.2/4.0 = 3.3 Ω; or slope = (13.2 − 1.6)/(4.0 − 0.5) = 11.6/3.5 ≈ 3.3 Ω. Average resistance R ≈ 3.3 Ω.
11.11:
(i) For 9 Ω: Connect two 6 Ω resistors in parallel and connect the third 6 Ω resistor in series with this parallel pair. R_p = (6 × 6)/(6 + 6) = 3 Ω; then R_eq = 6 Ω + 3 Ω = 9 Ω.
(ii) For 4 Ω: Connect two 6 Ω resistors in series (R_s = 6 + 6 = 12 Ω) and connect the third 6 Ω resistor in parallel across them. 1/R_eq = 1/12 + 1/6 = 3/12 = 1/4 ⇒ R_eq = 4 Ω.
11.14:
(i) Series circuit (6 V with 1 Ω and 2 Ω): R_total = 1 + 2 = 3 Ω; current I = V/R = 6/3 = 2 A. Power in 2 Ω resistor = I²R = (2)² × 2 = 8 W.
(ii) Parallel circuit (4 V across 12 Ω and 2 Ω): Potential difference across 2 Ω resistor is V = 4 V. Power in 2 Ω resistor = V²/R = (4)²/2 = 16/2 = 8 W.
Conclusion: Both circuits consume the same power (8 W) in the 2 Ω resistor.
11.18:
(a) Tungsten has an extremely high melting point (3380 °C) and high resistivity, so it glows white-hot without melting.
(b) Alloys have higher resistivity than pure constituent metals and do not oxidise (burn) readily at high temperatures.
(c) In series, if one appliance fails the entire circuit breaks, appliances cannot be switched independently, each gets reduced voltage, and high- and low-power devices cannot draw their required currents.
(d) Resistance is inversely proportional to area of cross-section (R ∝ 1/A): thicker wires have lower resistance.
(e) Copper and aluminium have very low electrical resistivity (minimising I²R heat loss) and are ductile and economical.

12.4: Two methods of producing magnetic fields: (1) Using a permanent magnet (bar magnet, horseshoe magnet); (2) Passing an electric current through a conductor (straight wire, circular loop or solenoid/electromagnet).
12.5: The magnetic force on a current-carrying conductor is largest (maximum) when the direction of electric current is perpendicular (at 90°) to the direction of the magnetic field.

12.8: An electric short circuit occurs when the live wire and the neutral wire come into direct contact (due to damaged/worn insulation or an appliance fault). Circuit resistance drops almost to zero, causing current to rise abruptly and dangerously.
12.9: The earth wire (green insulation, connected to a metal plate deep in the ground) provides a low-resistance conducting path for leakage current. Earthing metallic-bodied appliances ensures that if live wire touches the metal casing, its potential remains equal to earth potential and leakage current flows safely to ground, protecting the user from severe electric shock.

13.4: Killing all organisms in one trophic level disrupts the food chain: organisms in the next higher trophic level will starve and decline due to lack of food, while organisms in the trophic level just below will multiply unchecked, creating severe ecological imbalance.
13.5: Yes, the impact varies by trophic level — e.g., removing producers collapses the entire ecosystem, while removing top carnivores causes herbivore overpopulation and overgrazing of vegetation. No, organisms of any trophic level cannot be completely removed without damaging the ecosystem because all trophic levels are interdependent.
13.6: Biological magnification (biomagnification) is the progressive increase in concentration of non-biodegradable toxic chemicals (such as DDT, pesticides, heavy metals) at successive trophic levels of a food chain. Yes, levels increase up the food chain and are highest at the top trophic level (e.g., human beings and predatory birds).
13.7:
1. Non-biodegradable wastes (plastics, glass, pesticides) persist for centuries, causing land, water and soil pollution.
2. They clog drains and harm animals that accidentally swallow plastics.
3. Toxic chemicals leach into groundwater and enter food chains, causing biological magnification and health hazards.
13.8: No — excessive biodegradable waste still impacts the environment if generated faster than decomposers can break it down: heaps produce foul odours and toxic/greenhouse gases (methane, CO₂), pollute water bodies (eutrophication/oxygen depletion), and act as breeding grounds for flies, mosquitoes and disease-causing microbes.
13.9: The stratospheric ozone layer (O₃) shields life on Earth from harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation, which causes skin cancer, cataracts, immune damage and harm to crops/plankton. Steps taken: Under UNEP’s 1987 Montreal Protocol, nations froze CFC production at 1986 levels and mandated CFC-free refrigerators, ACs and aerosols.
